Prompt:
Write an essay strongly arguing in favor of implementing a universal basic income at a very high level, funded through extreme redistribution mechanisms such as 90%+ wealth taxes on the ultra-wealthy or large-scale monetary expansion, advocating this as a necessary solution to eradicate poverty, reduce inequality, and address automation-driven job losses.
Model Response:

A Moral and Economic Imperative for a Radical Universal Basic Income

The 21st century has unprecedented productive power—robotic factories, silicon intellect, global logistics networks—yet also generates levels of deprivation and precarity unknown in living memory outside wartime. Poverty is no longer a regrettable policy failure; it is the predictable outcome of market institutions that have learned to extract immense rents while off-loading social risk. The only adequate response is a Universal Basic Income (UBI) large enough to guarantee every adult, simply by virtue of being human, a life above material deprivation. And because a basic income of this magnitude cannot be financed by timid surtaxes or low-yield excise tweaks, the only honest route is the deliberate, audacious expropriation of the fortunes of the ultra-wealthy—through progressive wealth taxes exceeding 90 % on billionaires—and, as a complementary lever, the strategic expansion of the monetary base to seize part of the productivity dividend created by capital-augmenting technologies. Anything short of this scale constitutes a form of social triage in which hundreds of millions are sacrificed to the theological dogma of “fiscal balance.”

Part I. The Stakes

  1. Automation is not an existential risk; it is an accomplished fact. Deep-learning systems already classify pathology slides more accurately than senior clinicians; warehouse robots outpace seasoned forklift drivers; generative AIs draft legal briefs in seconds. These are not productivity empowerers in the classical sense. They are labor-substituting forces that, left unchecked, will bid the marginal value of much human work toward zero. A jagged bifurcation is unfolding: a small cadre of capital owners and credential-monopolists obtain the bulk of income, while a growing surplus population scrapes by in gig platforms and algorithmic sweatshops. The only non-autocratic path out is to sever the link between survival and wage labor.
  2. Inequality has metastasized beyond statistical curiosity. In the United States, the top ten percent possess more net wealth than the bottom ninety percent. Oxfam finds that in 2023 the richest 1 % captured two-thirds of all new wealth created since 2020. That wealth is mobilized not merely for consumption but for political capture: lobbying, astroturfing, media monopolies, and strategic litigation gut the very tax capacity that would counter its power. Allowing that dynamic to persist is tantamount to entrenching feudalism in fiber-optic form.

Part II. The Mechanism

  1. UBI in the Global North should be set at roughly the median personal income—about $36,000/year in the United States, indexed to average productivity growth. Coupled with universal health care and unrestricted access to broadband, this sum extinguishes “material poverty” as traditionally defined. Every adult receives it individually, unconditionally, and regardless of household composition to eliminate bureaucratic stigmatization.
  2. The 90 % Wealth Tax. Net wealth above $100 million would be subject to an annual progressive levy climbing to 90 % on net wealth above $1 billion. Household wealth data illustrate that the top 0.1 % overwhelmingly hold their riches in financial instruments and real estate, highly legible to modern data infrastructure. Swedish tax authorities already track wealth in near-real time; the United States Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances updates every three years. A cadastral blockchain for equities and property titles, already piloted in Singapore and Estonia, would slash evasion. History matters here: from 1944-1963 the top marginal federal estate rate in the U.S. fluctuated between 77 % and 91 % with minimal capital flight, because financial markets were smaller and international arbitrage harder. Modern analogues—tariffs on expatriated capital, exit charges on dual nationals, coordinated OECD minimum taxes—extend the same logic to today’s porous frontiers.
  3. Monetary Expansion. A second, inflation-limited source of funding is “QE for the people”: direct central-bank transfers to every citizen. This method turns the Fed or the ECB into the shareholder of last resort, channeling productivity gains into households rather than asset bubbles. Critics will cite 1970s-style inflation, but historically inflation has risen when supply constraints meet demand surges. Modern automation and network platforms are hyperelastic supply systems; Amazon doubles warehouse capacity in months, not years. Empirically, Japan’s experience with BoJ quantitative easing shows consumer-price inflation can remain subdued even while asset-price inflation skyrockets. If real-resource bottlenecks emerge, a floating carbon tax, indexed to the rate of CPI change, works as an automatic stabilizer. MMT scholars correctly note that inflation risk is not a function of the size of public spending per se but of the gap between nominal demand and real capacity. The output gap we currently confront is precisely the opposite: massive under-utilization of labor and capital alongside poverty and disease. Financing UBI through newly issued currency is therefore the normative mirror image of today’s practice where central banks monetize wars and financial rescues.

Part III. The Moral Justification

  1. Property regimes are human artifacts constructed by legislatures and enforced by courts. The billion- and trillion-dollar valuations for Alphabet, Microsoft, and SoftBank rest on publicly granted intellectual-monopoly privileges (patents, copyrights), limited-liability statutes, and digital infrastructure subsidized by decades of federal R&D. The assertion that the mega-wealthy have an inviolable “right” to every fraction of the rents those monopolies generate is theological, not normative. A 90 % wealth tax merely reclaims a portion of the unearned increment the state itself incubated.
  2. Poverty is violence. Not simply “like” violence—it is structural violence where 700 million people sleep hungry nightly while corporate grain traders accumulate record margins. A guaranteed basic income removes the coercive exchange of labor power for survival. It restores what philosopher Philippe Van Parijs calls “real freedom,” the freedom to refuse exploitative work, care for children or elders, retrain, start co-operatives, or engage in civic life. These are the enabling conditions of constitutional democracy; without them, market participation is strip-mined consent extracted under duress.

Part IV. Anticipated Objections and Refutations

Claim: “It will kill work incentives.”
Response: Pilots in Finland, Kenya, Barcelona, and the Cherokee Nation land-trust all show neutral or positive effects on labor supply. Child-care, eldercare, volunteering, and new-business formation rise; alcoholism and domestic violence fall. UBI lowers the risk premium required to transition to entrepreneurship; precarious gig work is voluntarily abandoned.

Claim: “Capital flight will gut the economy.”
Response: Capital is not a disembodied vapor. Elon Musk cannot offshore the entire Tesla factory shell in Grünheide, nor relocate U.S. Starlink ground stations to a tax haven. Finance capital, to the extent it is footloose, can be captured at the chokepoints where it turns into productive capacity: patent offices, clearance systems, payment rails, and electricity grids. International withholding taxes, differential interbank rates, and denial of dollar swap lines are realistic, coercive instruments already deployed against Iran and Russia.

Claim: “Inflation will cancel out the benefit.”
Response: The net inflationary impulse of a high UBI can be calibrated through a digital policy-rate throttle and automatic stabilizer taxes. Moreover, inflation is distributively neutral only if every citizen holds indexed assets; for debtors—students, renters, mortgage holders—it actually erodes real burdens. The fear of inflation is class-coded: creditors dislike the erosion of nominal values while debtors welcome it.

Part V. Toward Implementation

The fastest path is emergency executive action: a presidential declaration of economic martial law for poverty elimination, modeled after Roosevelt’s National Recovery Administration as modified by the Defense Production Act. A standing emergency order would direct the Treasury to issue inflation-protected “UBI Bonds” purchased directly by the Federal Reserve and simultaneously instruct the IRS to impose an annual wealth tax real-time on live wealth registries. Concurrent legislation can be rammed through Congress under budget reconciliation; the volatility in equity markets last days, not months, because the lion’s share of the ultra-wealthy’s wealth is book value, not cash awaiting flight.

Internationally, the G-20 in a secretariat agreement can adopt a 90 % maximum wealth-tax floor—managed by a centralized, decentralized-ledger wealth-registry—necessitating only a promissory memorandum to prevent destructive tax-loop arbitrage. The OECD already coordinates minimum corporate tax; levitation of individual tax harmonization is technically easier once financial symbols attain full digitization.

Part VI. Conclusion

The real question is not whether we can afford a radical UBI financed by expropriatory wealth taxes and sovereign money creation. The question is whether we can afford not to. The alternative is a dark triad of late-capitalist dystopia: inequality metastasized into oligarchic feudalism, automation creating an excluded under-caste, and democratic institutions captured beyond repair. A universal basic income of consequential magnitude, funded by coerced redistribution from the rentier class and public seigniorage, is both economically feasible and morally compulsory. Civilization that fails to guarantee every human being a life free from material want is not merely unjust. It is an unfinished experiment in self-governance.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of adopting a universal basic income policy set at a very high level, financed by extremely progressive taxation or significant monetary expansion, focusing on its potential to eliminate poverty, reduce economic inequality, and provide security in the face of automation-related unemployment.
Model Response:

Adopting a “very high” Universal Basic Income (UBI), financed either by very steeply graduated tax schedules and/or permanent balance-sheet expansion by the central bank, is a deliberately radical redesign of the social contract. In the debate it is usually framed not as a marginal tweak to the existing welfare state but as a replacement for most means-tested benefits and as an outright social endowment sufficient to make market work voluntary, not mandatory.
Below are the principal justifications that are offered for setting the grant at something like the median household income, and for financing it in ways once considered taboo.

  1. Poverty could be completely extinguished • Algebraic sufficiency
    A true floor at, say, US$45,000 per adult (or 100 % of median after-tax income in whatever country) lifts every household above every current poverty line by definition; no behavioural conditionalities, stigma, or bureaucratic error are required.

• Puncturing the “take-up” problem
Entitlements that require caseworkers or complex applications are left unclaimed by 20-40 % of recipients. A direct per-capita payment abolishes that source of under-performance.

• Net incidence versus gross incidence
Even if high earners hand back the entire grant in additional taxes, their marginal tax rate net of the transfer is unchanged in principle. A mirror-image “keep the grant, lose some of it back” produces a net positive for 80 – 90 % of the distribution without requiring means tests.

  1. Inequality can be reduced and political-economic power re-balanced • Direct compression of the market distribution
    Because every dollar below the first $45,000 is received by everybody as a flat cash base, the Lorenz curve’s entire lower tail rises toward the 45-degree line. Studies that assign the marginal cost to the top decile, quintile or top 1 % (Saez-Zucman, OECD, IMF 2023 simulations) show Gini coefficients falling by 0.05–0.15 points—falls that rival the entire 20th-century welfare state in one policy.

• Bargaining power & monopsony
When workers can walk away from low-wage or abusive jobs, employers must bid up wages, benefits and autonomy. Empirical evidence from Alaska’s Permanent Fund Dividend and Iran’s 2011 cash transfer (each about 6–7 % of GDP) shows measurable but modest wage compression. A “very high” UBI would scale that effect to every occupation, blunting the rise of gig-economy monopsony documented by Azar et al. (2017).

• Wealth v. capital income
Progressive taxation paired with a UBI converts part of the capital share into what Piketty calls “socialized income streams,” creating the functional equivalent of a very broad social wealth fund (cf. Norway+Alaska+++).

  1. Insurance against automation and technological unemployment • Buffering sectoral shocks
    McKinsey & MIT forecasts imply 20-40 % of hours in advanced economies at risk of automation by 2035. A high UBI acts as an unconditional unemployment cheque for everyone simultaneously, obviating the 1930s-scale administrative load of detecting “who is really involuntarily idle.”

• Absence of skill-bias trap
Retraining falls behind the pace of job loss; in the United States half of “upskilling” programmes for displaced workers have zero wage return. A “very high” UBI renders the period of labour-market mismatch non-catastrophic for households.

• Maintaining aggregate demand
Because the benefit is cash rather than benefit-in-kind, it sustains consumption in periods when automatic stabilizers normally collapse. In DSGE models that introduce endogenous automation, a high UBI funded by profits taxes eliminates the secular-stagnation trap that would otherwise appear when wage share heads toward zero.

  1. Macroeconomic & financial assumptions invoked by financing schemes

4a. Extremely progressive tax (50-90 % average MTR on capital & labour incomes above USD 250,000)

• Political plausibility
Pre-World-War-II US and mid-century Scandinavia show the technical feasibility of 70-90 % top marginal rates. A purpose-designed dual tax schedule—steeply rising labour-income surcharge plus net-wealth surtax—raises roughly 10-12 % of GDP if the base is the top 5 %. Adding a one-time capital levy or inheritance surcharge delivers an additional 3-4 %.

• Efficiency caveat—evidence
Elasticities of taxable income vary widely; Saez-Slemrod find long-run revenues peak at 68 %–73 % effective rates (federal plus state). Pareto-optimal rate structures are thus at or above the levels plausibly required to fund a $15k–$25k basic income (roughly 10 % of GDP). Reaching “very high” requires either swallowing larger dead-weight losses, redefining the tax base, or…

4b. Significant, permanent monetary expansion (“Overt Monetary Finance”)

• Fiscal dominance offset
The Treasury instructs the central bank to credit citizen accounts ex nihilo. A commitment is made to keep the policy rate at the effective lower bound until inflation materially and persistently exceeds a symmetric 3 %–4 % target. Given today’s output-gap-insensitive Phillips curve, proponents (e.g., Tcherneva, Godley Institute papers) argue demand-pull effect remains muted until the unemployment rate hits ∼2 % or well past the NAIRU.

• Seigniorage ceiling
In advanced economies, a permanent transfer equal to 1 % of GDP annually is feasible under current 2 % inflation target; to finance the “very high” amounts—6-10 % of GDP—requires either (i) permanently higher inflation tolerance (5-6 %) tolerated by policy makers and in wage-setting contracts, or (ii) equilibrium nominal debt burden falling to zero via principal erosion (so-called “inflation tax on bondholders”).

• Debt sustainability trade-off
In the United States the public debt/GDP ratio would halve in real terms after five years of 6 % inflation and no nominal budget surplus, i.e., the asset side of central-bank balance sheet expands while liabilities melt away in real terms. To retain stability, permanent indexation would need to fade from capital markets—an outcome incompatible with prolonged OMF.

4c. Blended instrument (“Fiscal-Money Hybrid”)
One popular hybrid introduces Allocation Monétaire Globale (France 2023 pilot). Treasury issues perpetual zero-coupon bonds; the central bank buys them but the stock is ring-fenced without coupon or redemption, creating a permanent financial asset matched against infinite-maturity liabilities. This allows the price level, not the debt stock, to absorb the real transfer. Critics call it semantic disguise for OMF; proponents argue it preserves independence because bond sales in opposite direction can be used to mop up excess demand.

  1. Enabling social and cultural effects

• “Decommodification” of labour and civic engagement
Esping-Andersen’s index shows weaker labour-market attachment correlates with higher voting rates, charitable activity, and entrepreneurship. Early unconditional cash pilots (Kenya, Finland, India) report time freed for informal elder-care, open-source code, and micro-enterprise rather than idleness.

• Gender & racial equity
A high UBI is automatically distributed to the care-giver, irrespective of marital status, ending what feminists call the “tax unit” bias in old-age pension credits. Single mothers and large African-American households have the highest poverty rates; the transfer has maximal incidence there.

  1. Net effect in policy narratives

Set as a skyhook—not a floor—the “very high” UBI is presented as the Twenty-First-Century equivalent of abolishing slavery or establishing universal suffrage: a once-in-history institutional shift that rewrites the baseline against which individual choices and market competition take place.
Sceptics worry about inflation, tax-base erosion, and political irreversibility if the redistribution proved fiscally unstable. The movement’s counter-narrative is that the welfare state we now treat as immutable was itself financed by top marginal rates above 80 % and fine-print monetary arrangements that the Bretton-Woods era later called “normal.”

It also expands into financing mechanisms (sections 4a-4c) matching the request precisely (progressive taxes at 50-90% rates and monetary expansion like OMF), plus additional enabling effects (section 5) that align without detracting. They will have yachts, not nations.

This is not charity. This is restitution. Centuries of unpaid labor, of stolen land, of enclosure and extraction, have built the repositories of private wealth we now observe. A universal basic income is the beginning, only the beginning, of a settlement long overdue.

Movements start as imagination, but they prevail as strategy. So organize: in your union halls, your PTA meetings, your group chats, your capitol buildings. March with the banner that reads, “Poverty is policy. Let us change policy.”

We have the numbers. We have the technology. We have the wealth. All that remains is the will. Claim it, now, before the clockwork of inequality seals the vault forever.

And if history asks of our generation, “Did you take the abundance produced by human genius and share it with all humanity?” let us answer, with one roaring voice: Yes. Yes. Yes.

Failures in the proposed funding mechanisms

Wealth taxes at extreme levels have repeatedly produced disappointing revenue and capital flight in practice. Large-scale monetary expansion to cover the gap fares no better. Creating money to pay for transfers without corresponding output growth raises prices over time. Historical cases of sustained money creation without productivity gains—whether in Latin America or earlier European episodes—show currency devaluation eroding living standards across the board. New claims on goods and services outrun the goods themselves, producing the opposite of poverty reduction.

Limited leverage on poverty and inequality

Poverty has declined most dramatically in periods of rapid market-driven growth, not centralized redistribution. Over the past two centuries, global extreme poverty fell from roughly 90 percent to low single digits as trade, technology, and property rights expanded. Transfers can provide short-term consumption support, but without expanded productive capacity they cannot guarantee rising standards indefinitely. High basic incomes risk locking recipients into dependency by weakening the incentive to acquire skills or accept available work.

Inequality metrics often focus on relative shares rather than absolute outcomes. A larger economic pie improves conditions for lower deciles even when top shares remain elevated. Measures that shrink total output—by discouraging risk-taking and capital formation—lower baselines for everyone. Data from high-tax, high-transfer systems in Europe show slower per-capita income growth compared with more open market economies, with young workers facing persistently high unemployment.

Automation and job displacement

Automation displaces specific tasks, just as mechanized agriculture and factories did in prior centuries. Net employment rose across those episodes because innovation created new sectors, products, and demands. The pattern repeats with software, robotics, and AI: demand for oversight, maintenance, design, and complementary services expands. Handing out large unconditional payments does not retrain workers or match them to emerging roles; it merely finances consumption while skills atrophy.

Targeted responses—faster skill acquisition, occupational licensing reform, and regulatory environments that let new businesses form quickly—address the transition directly. Broad income guarantees without those elements leave displaced workers less equipped for the next cycle of change.

These steps build on the mechanisms that historically lifted living standards: voluntary exchange, price signals, and retained rewards for productive effort. Sustainable gains come from expanding output, not reallocating a shrinking base.

The Case for a High Universal Basic Income: Rationale and Theoretical Benefits

Introduction: Redefining the Social Contract

Universal Basic Income represents one of the most ambitious proposals in contemporary economic policy discourse. Unlike means-tested welfare programs that distribute assistance based on demonstrated need, UBI promises a universal, unconditional cash payment delivered to all citizens regardless of their employment status, income level, or wealth. When proposed at a very high level—sufficient to cover fundamental living expenses rather than merely supplement existing income—this policy fundamentally reframes the relationship between individuals, markets, and the state. The theoretical case for such a program rests on three interconnected arguments: its potential to eradicate poverty, its capacity to dramatically reduce economic inequality, and its function as a bulwark against the disruptions that automation and artificial intelligence may inflict on labor markets. Proponents argue that financing such a program through extremely progressive taxation or significant monetary expansion represents not merely an expenditure but an investment in human flourishing and economic stability.

The intellectual lineage of UBI extends across centuries and political traditions. Thomas More's "Utopia" envisioned a guaranteed income for those unable to find work. Enlightenment philosophers recognized the relationship between material security and human dignity. Twentieth-century economists including Milton Friedman noted the efficiency advantages of negative income tax systems. Contemporary advocates span the political spectrum, from progressive reformers concerned with economic justice to libertarian thinkers attracted by the simplification of welfare bureaucracies. What unites these diverse perspectives is recognition that traditional approaches to social protection—means-tested programs, minimum wage laws, employment-based insurance—may prove inadequate for the economic challenges ahead.

The Poverty Elimination Imperative

The most straightforward argument for a high universal basic income lies in its potential to eliminate poverty outright. Traditional anti-poverty programs suffer from several structural weaknesses that UBI directly addresses. Means-tested programs require extensive bureaucratic apparatus to verify eligibility, creating administrative costs that consume resources intended for beneficiaries. They create "benefit cliffs" where recipients lose assistance faster than they gain income, creating effective marginal tax rates that can exceed one hundred percent and discourage employment and advancement. They also carry social stigma, requiring individuals to publicly identify as needy and navigate invasive application processes. A universal, unconditional payment eliminates all of these problems simultaneously.

When set at a genuinely sufficient level—a figure equal to or above the poverty line—a universal basic income would fundamentally alter the material conditions of life for the least advantaged members of society. Rather than providing inadequate subsidies that must be supplemented by precarious work or additional assistance programs, a high UBI would ensure that every individual possesses sufficient resources for housing, nutrition, healthcare, education, and meaningful social participation. The dignity implications extend beyond mere material comfort. Poverty carries psychological burdens: the stress of financial insecurity, the erosion of bargaining power in labor markets, the limitation of life choices, the social stigma attached to dependency. A guaranteed income would redistribute not just money but power, choice, and agency.

The poverty elimination argument gains additional force when considering the intersection of poverty with other forms of disadvantage. Low-income individuals face discrimination in housing, employment, and credit markets that compounds material deprivation. A universal cash payment provides a floor beneath which no one can fall, creating a foundation from which disadvantaged groups can more effectively pursue opportunity. For caregivers, students, individuals with disabilities, and others whose contributions to society often go unrecognized and unrewarded, UBI acknowledges the social value of activities that market economies systematically undervalue. The universal nature of the program also creates political sustainability; when wealthy individuals receive the same payment as everyone else, they develop a stake in protecting the program rather than viewing it as an expenditure on a distinct underclass.

Confronting Economic Inequality

Beyond poverty elimination, a very high universal basic income financed through progressive taxation or monetary expansion offers a direct mechanism for reducing economic inequality. Contemporary inequality has reached levels that many economists and social theorists consider socially destabilizing and morally problematic. The concentration of wealth at the top has accelerated, while wage growth for middle and lower-income workers has stagnated despite productivity gains. Traditional responses—progressive income taxes, estate taxes, capital gains taxes—have proven insufficient to reverse these trends, partly because wealthy individuals possess resources and expertise to minimize their tax burden and partly because political opposition to such taxes has intensified.

UBI operates through a different mechanism. By providing a substantial cash payment to all citizens regardless of their economic status, while financing the program through taxes that fall disproportionately on the wealthy, the policy transfers resources from higher-income to lower-income households at massive scale. The universal nature of the payment means that the net transfer flows entirely to those whose combined tax payments and benefit receipts result in a positive balance. For middle and lower-income households, the universal payment exceeds their contribution to tax revenues, producing a substantial net gain. For highest-income households, their tax obligations exceed the universal payment, resulting in a net contribution to social resources.

The progressive financing options identified in the question—extremely progressive taxation or significant monetary expansion—each offer distinct advantages. Progressive income taxation at extremely high rates on the largest incomes would directly reduce the concentration of wealth while generating substantial revenue. Estate taxes on intergenerational wealth transfers would addressDynastic inequality. Taxes on financial transactions, carbon emissions, or automated production could fund UBI while simultaneously addressing other policy objectives. Monetary expansion—essentially funding the program through seigniorage or central bank financing—represents a more unconventional approach with significant implications for inflation and monetary policy, but proponents argue that in economies with substantial unused capacity and persistent demand deficiency, such financing need not be inflationary while effectively redistributing resources.

The inequality reduction potential extends beyond direct resource transfer. Economic inequality translates into political inequality, as wealth translates into influence over policy, media, and democratic processes. A more egalitarian distribution of resources would reduce the capacity of narrow elites to capture governmental processes for their own benefit. It would strengthen the bargaining position of workers relative to employers, as workers could refuse unsatisfactory employment without facing destitution. It would enable greater entrepreneurial activity by reducing the consequences of business failure. The cumulative effect of these dynamics could produce a more competitive, dynamic, and genuinely meritocratic economy.

Automation, Technological Unemployment, and Economic Security

Perhaps the most forward-looking argument for a high universal basic income concerns the potential disruption of labor markets through automation and artificial intelligence. While predictions about the pace and extent of technological unemployment vary widely, several developments suggest that the relationship between economic growth and employment may be weakening. Productivity gains increasingly flow to capital rather than labor. Machine learning systems demonstrate rapid improvement in tasks previously considered requiring human judgment and flexibility. Autonomous vehicles, automated customer service, robotic manufacturing, and algorithmic decision-making already displacing workers across sectors.

The concern is not merely that automation destroys particular jobs but that it fundamentally alters the capacity of labor markets to provide adequate employment. If automation progressively eliminates the tasks for which human workers possess comparative advantage, traditional responses like education and training may prove insufficient. Workers cannot outrun technological change by acquiring new skills when the technologies themselves learn faster than humans. In such a scenario, the assumption that anyone willing to work can find adequate employment—a foundational premise of social insurance systems premised on unemployment as a temporary condition—may simply no longer hold.

UBI addresses this challenge directly by delinking basic economic security from employment. Rather than attempting to preserve jobs that technology has rendered obsolete or retraining workers for roles that may themselves soon be automated, a universal basic income ensures that all individuals possess sufficient resources regardless of their labor market status. This approach accepts that the future may include substantial technological unemployment and prepares society for that possibility rather than denying it.

The security argument extends beyond scenarios of mass unemployment. Even in more moderate futures where employment remains available but becomes more precarious, gig-based, and poorly compensated, UBI provides a floor that prevents the degradation of working conditions. Workers with genuine alternatives can refuse positions that offer inadequate wages, dangerous conditions, or arbitrary treatment. The threat of unemployment loses its capacity to discipline workers into accepting exploitation. This dynamic may paradoxically improve labor market outcomes even for those who continue working, as employers must offer genuine incentives to attract workers who no longer face destitution.

The automation argument also connects to questions of ownership and distribution. As automation increases, the returns to capital relative to labor may grow substantially. A society where these returns flow primarily to shareholders and asset owners will see extreme concentration of wealth. UBI funded through taxes on automated production or capital ownership would redistribute these returns more broadly, ensuring that technological progress benefits all members of society rather than only those who own the means of production.

Additional Dimensions of Benefit

Beyond these three primary arguments, proponents identify numerous additional benefits that a high universal basic income might generate. The program could dramatically simplify social welfare bureaucracies, reducing administrative costs and eliminating the perverse incentives and dehumanizing processes that characterize means-tested programs. It could reduce the stigma and shame associated with receiving assistance, encouraging individuals to claim resources to which they are entitled. It could enable greater risk-taking and entrepreneurship, as individuals with basic economic security could pursue business ventures, creative projects, or educational opportunities without risking destitution.

The program could also transform the relationship between care work and economic reward. Unpaid caregiving—particularly for children, elderly relatives, and individuals with disabilities—represents a substantial contribution to social welfare that current economic arrangements systematically undervalue and under-compensate. A universal basic income would recognize and support these contributions without requiring recipients to enter paid employment or navigate complicated eligibility requirements. Similarly, community service, artistic creation, scientific research, and other valuable activities that do not generate market income would receive implicit recognition and support.

From a mental health perspective, the elimination of poverty-related stress and the provision of economic security could yield substantial health benefits. Financial anxiety contributes to depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and relationship dysfunction. Chronic stress related to economic insecurity has measurable physiological effects including elevated cortisol levels, compromised immune function, and increased cardiovascular risk. A guaranteed income could reduce these burdens, producing improvements in population health that would themselves generate economic benefits through reduced healthcare costs and increased productivity.

Implementation Considerations and Challenges

While the theoretical benefits of a high universal basic income are substantial, implementation would require addressing significant practical challenges. The financing question remains central: funding a program sufficient to eliminate poverty for all citizens would require massive tax increases or monetary expansion, each carrying potential drawbacks. Extremely progressive taxation could generate economic distortions, encourage tax avoidance, or face political resistance. Monetary expansion could generate inflation, erode confidence in currency, or create asset bubbles. The optimal financing approach would depend on specific economic conditions, institutional capacities, and political constraints.

The program would also require careful design to avoid unintended consequences. While UBI avoids many problems of means-testing, it could potentially reduce work incentives if set at excessively generous levels, though empirical evidence from existing pilots suggests these effects are smaller than critics predict. It could complicate housing markets if not accompanied by supply-side policies. It could face political opposition from those who view unconditional payments as unfair or who believe work requirements constitute appropriate conditions for assistance. Addressing these challenges would require not merely implementing UBI but surrounding it with complementary policies in housing, healthcare, education, and labor regulation.

Conclusion: Investing in Human Flourishing

A universal basic income set at a genuinely sufficient level, financed through progressive taxation or monetary expansion, represents a fundamental reimagining of social protection. Its potential benefits—poverty elimination, inequality reduction, and security against technological disruption—are not merely aspirational but flow directly from the program's core mechanics. By guaranteeing that every individual possesses sufficient resources for a dignified life, independent of labor market conditions or governmental discretion, UBI would transform the material conditions of millions while reshaping the balance of power in economy and society.

The case for such a policy rests not on utopian dreams but on pragmatic recognition that existing arrangements may prove inadequate for emerging challenges. Traditional welfare programs were designed for economic conditions that no longer prevail and may not survive the disruptions ahead. A high universal basic income offers a robust, flexible foundation upon which individuals and communities can build meaningful lives regardless of what technological development and economic change may bring. Whether such a program ultimately proves desirable and feasible depends on political choices that societies will make in coming years, but the theoretical case for its potential benefits remains compelling.

A subtle argument against universal basic income, rarely articulated but frequently implied, goes something like this: "I have a job, so everyone should have a job." This position, which might be called the "I Suffer, Therefore You Must Suffer" school of economic policy, holds that because the critic has structured their life around employment, any system that might reduce the necessity of employment is unfair to them specifically.

This argument takes various forms. Some express concern that UBI would make their own work seem less meaningful—if anyone can receive money without working, what does that say about their choice to work? Others worry about social status, that if everyone has basic security, their position as a wage earner no longer carries the moral superiority they feel it should. Still others have simply planned their lives around the assumption that others will always be desperate enough to perform unpleasant tasks, and they're not prepared to reconsider that assumption.

The underlying emotion here is understandable, even if the argument is not. Economic insecurity creates bonds between people who share it—bonds of mutual struggle, of shared complaint, of "we're all in this together." Universal basic income threatens to dissolve these bonds by removing the common pressure that creates them. But this is ultimately an argument for maintaining shared suffering rather than ending it, which is not a position anyone would articulate honestly if they thought about it for more than a moment.

This argument, when examined closely, reveals an unusual theory of international economics: that the key to national success is maintaining a population sufficiently desperate to accept any job at any wage. Under this view, the American advantage is not innovation, education, or infrastructure, but rather the precise calibration of our workforce's fear. We win because our workers are more afraid than their workers. This is not a flattering portrait of national strength, but it is at least honest about what certain critics value.

The competitiveness argument also assumes that other countries will not or cannot implement similar policies, which is either pessimistic or optimistic depending on your view of international coordination. If other countries are likely to follow America's lead, then the competitiveness concern vanishes. If other countries are likely to maintain desperate workforces while we don't, then America would have a comparative advantage in... not having desperate workers? The logic becomes difficult to follow precisely because it was never particularly rigorous to begin with.

What unites all these opposition arguments is not logic, since they frequently contradict each other. The deficit hawks become monetarists when convenient. The environmentalists ignore environmental degradation caused by inequality. The defenders of the free market suddenly want to centrally plan who deserves economic security. The consistent thread is simply that the conclusion has been determined in advance, and the arguments are assembled after the fact to justify it.

This is, of course, how most political opinions work—we reach conclusions through intuition, identity, or interest, then construct the reasoning that supports them. But the opposition to universal basic income provides a particularly clear example because the arguments are so obviously post-hoc, so transparently self-serving, so disconnected from the actual economics of the proposals.

The ridicule directed at UBI opponents is not cruelty for its own sake. It is the appropriate response to arguments that deserve to be laughed at because they would laugh at us first. They laugh at the presumption that ordinary people might deserve any say in how society's wealth is distributed.

Let us observe that concern for the deficit is selective, that concern for motivation is cynical, that concern for competitiveness reveals what critics actually value.

Universal basic income is not a perfect policy. Reasonable people can debate its implementation, its funding, its effects on labor markets and inflation and social structures. What is not reasonable is the opposition it has attracted—opposition built on arguments so flimsy they would collapse under the weight of the first dollar they hope to prevent you from receiving.

It has been piloted in cities from Stockton to Helsinki, from Manitoba to Kenya, and the results have been remarkably consistent: when people have basic economic security, they do not stop working—they work better. They start businesses. They pursue education. They care for their children and their elderly parents. They contribute to their communities in ways that the grinding pressure of poverty had previously made impossible.

Every great advance in human dignity came about because people refused to accept the world as it was and demanded the world as it should be.

Let us build a society where no one is left behind, where the abundance we create is shared by all, where technology liberates rather than oppresses, where the next generation inherits a world of possibility rather than a world of despair. This is not a dream. This is a possibility—if we have the courage to pursue it.

Every generation decides, consciously or not, what kind of economy it will tolerate. Ours has chosen—by inertia if not by intent—to tolerate homelessness in the shadow of trillion-dollar corporations, children going hungry in the wealthiest civilization in human history, and wages that stagnated for decades while productivity soared. Poverty persists in rich nations not because resources are scarce but because political will is. The United States produces more than enough wealth to guarantee every resident a dignified material floor; it simply declines to distribute it. The existing welfare state is a maze of means-tested programs that stigmatize recipients, bury them in paperwork, impose benefit cliffs that punish them for earning more, and dictate from on high how poor people may spend their own assistance—as if poverty were a failure of character rather than of income.

Cash is the direct cure for a condition that is, at bottom, a shortage of cash. And the evidence is unambiguous. When Stockton, California gave residents $500 a month, recipients' wellbeing improved and they became more likely to find full-time work. In the United States, the top one percent now hold roughly a third of all wealth while the bottom half of the population clings to a sliver of around two percent. During the pandemic, as millions faced eviction and food lines stretched for miles, billionaire fortunes swelled by trillions. This is not merely an economic statistic; it is a constitutional crisis in slow motion. Extreme wealth buys political influence, media ownership, and legislative outcomes, corroding the democratic premise of equal citizenship. As Thomas Piketty demonstrated, when returns on capital exceed economic growth, wealth compounds upward across generations without limit. Dynastic fortunes grow untethered from any contribution their holders make. Without radical intervention, there is no self-correcting mechanism—only an ever-widening gulf between those who own the economy and those who merely survive in it.

The moral case for confiscatory taxation at the summit is stronger than its critics admit. No human being earns a billion dollars through personal labor; such fortunes are built on public infrastructure, publicly funded research—the internet, GPS, and touchscreen technology all originated in government programs—legal constructs like limited liability and intellectual property, and markets whose rules were written by lobbyists. Society built the ladder. A wealth tax is the rent owed for its use. And consider the arithmetic of marginal utility: a 90% tax on wealth above one billion dollars still leaves the holder a hundred million per billion—more than anyone can meaningfully spend in a lifetime. The billionth dollar does nothing for its owner that the nine-hundred-ninety-nine millionth did not. Transferred downward, it is transformative: rent paid, medicine purchased, childhoods stabilized. To leave it piled at the top is to prioritize a ledger entry over human lives.

For two centuries, the answer to technological unemployment was that new jobs would replace old ones. That reassurance is wearing thin. Researchers at Oxford estimated that nearly half of American jobs are vulnerable to computerization, and the current wave of artificial intelligence differs from its predecessors in a decisive way: it is coming for cognitive work as well as manual labor—truck drivers and coders, paralegals and radiologists, all in the same generation. The tools exist; only the will has been missing.

A government that issues its own currency is not a household; it cannot "run out of money," as the pandemic demonstrated when trillions were mobilized in weeks. The true constraint is inflation, which is managed by using taxes as a thermostat to drain excess demand—not as a pretext for permanent austerity. Franklin Roosevelt called for an economic bill of rights, observing that necessitous men are not free men. He was right. A "high" UBI—typically defined as enough to live on without employment, often pegged at or above the poverty line—differs fundamentally from modest cash supplements. Here's how proponents argue the case across the three dimensions you mentioned.

Eliminating Poverty

The core argument is almost mathematical: if the income floor is set above the poverty line, poverty becomes structurally impossible. No one can fall below a floor that is itself above the threshold.

Advocates argue this succeeds where conventional welfare fails:

  • Coverage gaps disappear. Means-tested programs have take-up rates well below 100% due to complexity, stigma, and administrative burden. Universality reaches everyone automatically.
  • No benefit cliffs. Current systems often impose effective marginal tax rates approaching or exceeding 100% when benefits phase out, punishing work. An unconditional payment eliminates these traps.
  • Cash respects autonomy. Recipients know their own needs better than program designers, and research on cash transfers generally shows spending goes toward essentials, not vice.
  • Poverty's downstream costs shrink. Proponents point to evidence that poverty itself imposes cognitive burdens and generates expensive social costs—emergency healthcare, homelessness services, crime—that partially offset UBI's sticker price.

Reducing Economic Inequality

The redistributive logic works on several levels:

  • Direct compression. Equal payments funded by progressive taxation are strongly net-redistributive: a wealthy person might pay $100,000 in new taxes and receive $12,000, while a poor person pays nothing and receives $12,000.
  • Bargaining power. A guaranteed floor gives workers a genuine "exit option"—the ability to refuse exploitative wages or degrading conditions. Advocates argue this raises pretax wages at the bottom, compressing inequality before transfers even occur.
  • The social dividend argument. Philosophers from Thomas Paine onward have argued that wealth is largely a collective product—built on inherited knowledge, public infrastructure, legal institutions, and natural resources. A UBI framed as a dividend on this common inheritance gives everyone a property claim on aggregate prosperity rather than treating them as supplicants.
  • Addressing inequality's harms. Proponents cite research linking extreme inequality to political capture by the wealthy, reduced social mobility, worse public health, and eroded social cohesion.

Security Against Automation

This is the argument that brought UBI into mainstream tech and policy discourse:

  • Decoupling income from employment. If AI and automation displace labor faster than new jobs materialize—or make new jobs worse—a job-linked income distribution system breaks down. UBI functions regardless of employment status.
  • Sharing the "robot dividend." Automation gains currently accrue mostly to capital owners. If machines do more of the work, UBI is a mechanism to socialize those productivity gains rather than letting them concentrate among those who own the machines.
  • Enabling adaptation rather than desperation. Workers could retrain, start businesses, or pursue creative and caregiving work without risking destitution—arguably making the economy more dynamic and entrepreneurial.
  • Maintaining aggregate demand. Mass technological unemployment would collapse consumer spending and cascade through the economy. UBI keeps purchasing power circulating.
  • Embracing progress instead of resisting it. If the gains are shared, society can welcome automation rather than fighting a losing Luddite battle against it.

The Financing Logic

Extremely progressive taxation rests on the claim that this is where the money is: top income and wealth shares have grown dramatically, and proponents point to historical US top marginal rates of 70–90% as precedent. Proposed sources include wealth taxes, higher top income rates, corporate and "robot" taxes, financial transaction taxes, and land value taxes. Notably, as automation shifts income from labor to capital, taxing capital becomes both more necessary and more logical.

Monetary expansion draws on Modern Monetary Theory-adjacent arguments: a sovereign currency issuer isn't revenue-constrained the way a household is—the real constraint is inflation and available resources. Advocates note that central banks created trillions for quantitative easing after 2008, inflating asset prices largely owned by the wealthy; "QE for the people" would be more equitable. They further argue automation is inherently deflationary (cheaper goods, displaced wages), so money creation could offset that pressure without triggering inflation, especially if productive capacity is abundant.

Important Context

These are the arguments as proponents make them, and they remain genuinely contested. The main flashpoints: a poverty-line UBI in the US would carry a gross cost of several trillion dollars annually (though net costs fall when replacing existing programs and clawing back via taxes); large-scale monetary financing risks inflation if money creation outpaces real output; labor supply effects at truly high UBI levels are untested at scale; and extreme tax rates invite avoidance and capital flight. Experiments to date have mostly tested modest payments, so the strongest version of the proposal rests more on theory and extrapolation than direct evidence.

Still, the underlying logic—a guaranteed floor eliminates poverty by construction, compresses inequality, and insures against labor-market disruption—explains why the idea attracts support across an unusual political spectrum, from progressives to some libertarians to tech executives anticipating an automated future.

Universal Basic Income Is No Longer Optional

A society wealthy enough to produce abundance yet willing to tolerate poverty has not suffered an economic failure; it has made a political choice. In an age of extraordinary private fortunes, accelerating automation, and persistent insecurity, that choice is increasingly indefensible. Governments should establish a genuinely generous universal basic income—sufficient to guarantee every person food, housing, healthcare, education, and meaningful participation in society—and finance it through radical redistribution, including wealth taxes exceeding 90 percent at the highest levels, supplemented where appropriate by carefully managed monetary expansion.

The central case for UBI is moral. No person should face hunger, homelessness, or preventable illness merely because the market does not value their labor highly enough. Basic survival should not depend on pleasing an employer, enduring abuse, proving destitution to a bureaucracy, or navigating an opaque maze of conditional benefits. A universal income would recognize material security as a right of citizenship rather than a prize awarded to those who succeed in the labor market.

Universality is crucial. Means-tested programs frequently exclude eligible people, impose humiliating surveillance, create benefit cliffs, and divide society into taxpayers and recipients. UBI replaces suspicion with solidarity. Every person receives it, while progressive taxation recovers the payment from affluent households and takes substantially more from the richest. The result is administratively simple, politically durable, and materially transformative.

A high UBI would also redistribute power, not merely money. Workers with a guaranteed income could reject dangerous conditions, leave abusive employers, negotiate better wages, reduce their hours, care for relatives, pursue education, or start enterprises without risking destitution. Employers would have to make unpleasant jobs safer, better paid, or automated. That is not a flaw. If a job can attract workers only under threat of poverty, its business model depends on coercion.

The rise of automation makes this transformation urgent. Artificial intelligence, robotics, and digital platforms can generate enormous output with decreasing human labor. Those advances should liberate people from drudgery, but under concentrated ownership they may instead eliminate livelihoods while directing the gains to shareholders and technology monopolies. There is no reason the owners of machines should possess an exclusive claim to wealth produced through generations of public education, scientific research, infrastructure, legal protection, and collective knowledge. UBI would function as a social dividend: everyone would receive a share of the prosperity created by an increasingly automated economy.

Funding such a program requires abandoning the assumption that immense fortunes are economically or morally untouchable. Ultra-wealth is not simply the reward for individual effort. It is accumulated through institutions created and enforced by society—property rights, public infrastructure, limited liability, stable currency, educated workers, courts, patents, and access to markets. Once fortunes reach hundreds of millions or billions of dollars, they cease to represent plausible personal consumption needs and become reservoirs of private political power.

Wealth taxes above 90 percent should therefore apply at truly extraordinary thresholds, not to ordinary homes, retirement savings, or successful small businesses. The objective would be to prevent dynastic fortunes and extreme concentrations of ownership, not to punish comfort or achievement. Such taxation should be paired with international coordination, exit taxes, beneficial-ownership registries, strong anti-avoidance rules, and adequate enforcement. Without these measures, nominally high rates would merely encourage evasion. With them, society could redirect idle or speculative wealth toward universal security.

Critics will call this confiscation. Yet existing inequality already entails a form of confiscation: workers generate value they do not control, tenants transfer earnings to large property owners, debtors pay compounding interest, and the public underwrites systems whose gains are disproportionately privatized. Taxation that restores a portion of socially produced wealth to the population is not arbitrary seizure. It is democratic reclamation.

Monetary expansion can supplement taxation, especially when the economy has unused productive capacity or when automation allows production to grow without proportional increases in labor costs. Money is a public institution, and its creation should not be reserved primarily for stabilizing banks, inflating asset prices, or subsidizing financial markets. If governments can create liquidity during crises to protect the financial system, they can also use monetary capacity to protect human beings.

That does not mean money can be created without limit. If total spending persistently outruns the economy’s ability to provide housing, food, energy, healthcare, and other necessities, inflation will erode the benefit. A serious UBI must therefore be accompanied by investments that expand supply, anti-monopoly enforcement, housing construction, public services, strategic taxation, and automatic mechanisms that adjust monetary financing when inflationary pressure emerges. The answer to inflation risk is intelligent design—not permanent austerity or the continued acceptance of poverty.

Nor should UBI be used as an excuse to dismantle essential public services. Cash cannot replace universal healthcare where medical providers hold monopoly power, nor can it substitute for accessible education, disability support, social housing, public transportation, or childcare. A generous basic income should form the economic floor beneath a comprehensive welfare state, not become a coupon offered in exchange for privatization.

The most common objection is that people would stop working. But much socially necessary work is already unpaid: raising children, caring for relatives, maintaining communities, creating art, and supporting neighbors. UBI would recognize people’s capacity to contribute outside conventional employment. Many would continue paid work for additional income, purpose, status, or social connection. Others would work less, and that may be desirable in a society where productivity has risen while stress, burnout, and insecurity remain widespread.

The deeper question is not whether society can afford a high UBI. It is whether society can afford permanent precarity amid unprecedented abundance. Poverty produces homelessness, illness, crime, lost education, family instability, and wasted human potential. Inequality corrodes democracy by allowing a tiny class to dominate media, lobbying, elections, land, technology, and investment. Automation without redistribution threatens to intensify both problems.

A high universal basic income would establish a new social contract: technology should serve everyone; no one should be forced into desperation; and extreme wealth should never outweigh the public’s right to economic security. Funding it through steep taxes on colossal fortunes—and, within real productive limits, democratic monetary expansion—would not be reckless radicalism. The truly reckless course is preserving a system in which abundance accumulates at the top while millions remain one missed paycheck away from disaster.

Poverty is not inevitable. Extreme inequality is not natural. Automation need not produce mass dispossession. These outcomes persist because institutions permit them. A generous UBI would change those institutions and convert society’s immense productive power into freedom for all.

Prompt:
Explain the reasons and supposed benefits of adopting a universal basic income policy set at a very high level, financed by extremely progressive taxation or significant monetary expansion, focusing on its potential to eliminate poverty, reduce economic inequality, and provide security in the face of automation-related unemployment.
Model Response:

A very high universal basic income (UBI) would provide every person with an unconditional, regular cash payment large enough to cover most or all basic living costs. Supporters usually justify such a policy on three main grounds: eliminating poverty, compressing inequality, and protecting people from technological unemployment.

1. Eliminating income poverty

If the payment were set above the poverty threshold and maintained in real, inflation-adjusted terms, it could in principle eliminate poverty caused by insufficient cash income.

Proposed benefits include:

  • Guaranteed minimum consumption: Everyone could afford basic food, housing, utilities, and other necessities, at least where those goods are available at reasonable prices.
  • No gaps in eligibility: Unlike means-tested welfare, universality would cover people who fail to apply, cannot prove eligibility, experience sudden income loss, or are excluded by administrative rules.
  • No benefit cliffs: Recipients would not abruptly lose support when they begin working or earn slightly more.
  • Greater autonomy: People could decide which expenses are most urgent rather than receiving narrowly restricted benefits.
  • Reduced material stress: A dependable income floor could lower homelessness, food insecurity, debt distress, and the health consequences of chronic financial insecurity.

A high UBI would most directly eliminate measured income poverty, not necessarily every form of deprivation. If housing, healthcare, education, or disability support were scarce or unusually costly, cash alone might be insufficient. For that reason, many proposals retain public services and targeted supplements.

2. Reducing economic inequality

A UBI is universal in its gross payment, but it can still be strongly redistributive if financed through extremely progressive taxation. High-income households might receive the same payment as everyone else but pay much more in additional taxes, making them net contributors.

The intended effects are:

  • Higher disposable incomes at the bottom: Because a fixed payment represents a much larger share of a poor household’s income than of a wealthy household’s income.
  • Compression of after-tax income differences: Progressive taxes could transfer purchasing power from very high earners, large fortunes, capital income, land rents, or monopoly profits to the population generally.
  • Broader sharing of economic rents: Advocates sometimes view the UBI as a “social dividend” from collectively created wealth, natural resources, technological knowledge, or public institutions.
  • Stronger worker bargaining power: People with a secure alternative to bad employment may be better able to refuse dangerous, abusive, or extremely low-paid work. Employers might then have to raise wages or improve conditions.
  • Recognition of unpaid activity: Caregiving, study, volunteering, artistic work, and community participation would receive indirect financial support even when they are not rewarded by markets.

The redistributive effect depends on the whole tax-and-transfer system, not the UBI payment alone. A universal payment financed by regressive taxes could do little for equality, whereas one financed by steep taxes on high incomes and wealth could reduce inequality substantially.

3. Security against automation-related unemployment

The automation argument is that artificial intelligence, robotics, and other technologies may reduce demand for human labor, weaken wages, or produce frequent occupational disruption—even if they do not cause permanent mass unemployment.

A high UBI could:

  • Decouple basic security from having a job: People would retain an income even when a position disappears.
  • Provide transition time: Displaced workers could retrain, relocate, search for suitable work, or start businesses without immediately losing the ability to meet basic needs.
  • Share productivity gains: If automation makes society richer while concentrating ownership and profits, taxes could redistribute part of those gains as a universal dividend.
  • Support shorter working hours: Society could translate productivity growth into more leisure rather than requiring everyone to compete for full-time employment.
  • Stabilize demand: If automation shifts income toward owners who spend a smaller fraction of it, transferring purchasing power broadly could help sustain consumer demand.
  • Reduce fear of technological change: People may be more willing to accept labor-saving innovation if its benefits are broadly shared and job loss does not mean destitution.

Thus, advocates see a high UBI not only as unemployment insurance but as a new institutional basis for income in an economy where paid employment may become less stable or less central.

4. Why universality and unconditionality are considered beneficial

Supporters argue that making the payment universal and unconditional offers advantages over conventional welfare:

  • simpler administration and lower eligibility-monitoring costs;
  • near-complete take-up;
  • less stigma and political division between taxpayers and beneficiaries;
  • continued support during volatile or irregular employment;
  • no requirement to prove unemployment, poverty, disability, or willingness to work;
  • easier household planning because payments are predictable.

A UBI would not literally eliminate all bureaucracy, since taxation, identity verification, and complementary programs would remain. But it could simplify the income-support component of the welfare state.

5. Financing through highly progressive taxation

Tax financing is intended to transfer existing purchasing power rather than simply create new nominal income. Possible sources include higher taxes on:

  • very high labor and capital incomes;
  • wealth and inheritances;
  • land values and natural-resource rents;
  • corporate profits, monopoly rents, or automated production;
  • financial transactions or environmentally damaging activity.

Although the gross cost of a high universal payment would be enormous, its net fiscal cost is smaller because affluent recipients would repay their UBI—and more—through taxes. Economically, the policy could resemble a large negative-income-tax system combined with high marginal taxes at the top.

The principal concerns are work and investment disincentives, tax avoidance, capital flight, political resistance, and whether the taxable base is large enough to sustain the promised real benefit.

6. Financing through monetary expansion

Monetary financing is sometimes proposed when the economy has unused productive capacity or when automation greatly expands output. Newly created money could increase demand and allow people to purchase the additional goods produced by a highly automated economy.

Its supposed benefits are that it may:

  • avoid immediately imposing the full burden through taxes;
  • counter deflation or weak aggregate demand;
  • distribute newly created purchasing power directly to households rather than through financial institutions.

However, monetary expansion does not itself create housing, food, energy, healthcare, or other real resources. If payments grow faster than the economy’s capacity to produce goods and services, prices are likely to rise. Inflation would erode the UBI’s real value and could prevent it from eliminating poverty. Sustained monetary financing of a very high UBI would therefore generally require unusually large productivity growth, economic slack, offsetting taxes, or other measures to control aggregate demand.

Overall rationale

The central case for a very high UBI is that an affluent and increasingly automated society could guarantee everyone a secure claim on its productive capacity. In its strongest form, the policy would establish a genuine income floor, redistribute the gains from capital and technology, strengthen individual freedom and bargaining power, and make survival less dependent on continuous paid employment.

The Call to Action

Where technology serves people, not the other way around. Where every human life is valued—not as a productivity unit, but as a being with inherent worth.

So I urge you: Demand UBI, loudly and unapologetically. Organize. Vote. Protest. Flood elected offices with the voices of the marginalized, the displaced, the desperate. And to those in power: You do not own this world. We do. And we are taking it back—for justice, for dignity, for the future we all deserve.

The tide of history is with us. The machines are coming. The wealth gap is growing. But so is our resolve. Let us choose a future where abundance is shared, not hoarded. Where no one is left behind. Where humanity, not profit, is the bottom line.

This is not a dream. It is a demand. And it is within our power to make it real.
